_comment: Eastern Cape Department of Education Grade 11 Geography P2 (Development Geography, Resources and Sustainability and Geographical Skills and Techniques), November 2024 provincial common examination.
Questions and marking-guideline answers extracted from the text layer of the official PDFs
(paper2.pdf, paper2_memo.pdf) and read against the rendered pages. Figures, maps,
graphs and photographs are described in [FIGURE: ...] brackets inside 'context'. memo_answer is
from the official marking guideline (English); mark allocations such as (2) are kept, one
accepted point per line. Column A/B items use the Grade 12 '[Y ... / Z ...]' style.
FORMAT: Section A Question 1 Development (60) and Question 2 Resources and Sustainability (60);
Section B Question 3 Geographical Skills and Techniques (30) on a 1:50 000 topographical map and a
1:10 000 orthophoto map of Mbombela. All three questions are compulsory (150). The map sheets were
not published with the paper, so map-read inputs come from the memo's accepted values. Question 1.1
uses the letters X and Z (not Y and Z) for COLUMN B. Sub-parts (a)/(b) are kept in one entry.

questions.context: 1.3 Refer to the extract below on rural community development. EMPOWERING RURAL COMMUNITIES: INVESTING IN WOMEN: Rural communities and rural women in particular, bear the largest burden of poverty in South Africa. The main factors contributing to the poverty of rural women include low literacy and skills training and poor access to services, especially healthcare. Investing in women is an imperative to development. Women often have different needs than men due to their societal standing, as well as continuing imbalance in the divisions of labour for managing or undertaking domestic tasks, such as taking care of or raising children. The Kwanalu's Women and Youth in Rural Entrepreneurship (WYRE) initiative aims to strengthen KZN's rural and farming communities. Its goal is to build productive and sustainable family and community livelihoods. Through WYRE's programme, women who are part of the community development programme receive the following support: [FIGURE: four icons: AGRICULTURAL TRAINING; FINANCIAL AND BUSINESS MANAGEMENT TRAINING; ACCESS TO FINANCE; NETWORKING: LINKING WOMEN ACROSS AFRICA.] The WYRE programme is not only enhancing the skills and leadership qualities of its participants, but is also playing a crucial role in the sustainable development of rural economies in KZN, fostering a new generation of entrepreneurial leaders in agriculture. [Adapted from www.foodformzansi.co.za/-kwanalu-empowers-rural-entrepreneurs-in-kzn/]

questions.context: 1.5 Refer to the cartoon and extract on development aid. [FIGURE: cartoon of a large tank labelled 'AFRICA AID' whose pipes leak into branches labelled GRAFT, CRIME, CORRUPTION, DICTATORS, THEFT and WASTE, with only a trickle reaching a man holding a bowl at the end.] FOREIGN AID: IMPACT ON DEVELOPMENT: Over the decades, billions of dollars have been channelled from wealthier nations to poorer ones in the hope of promoting economic growth, alleviating poverty and enhancing the people's quality of life. However, a complex and often disappointing reality emerges: despite these efforts, many developing countries continue to struggle with high levels of poverty. Despite receiving $36 billion annually in aid, Sub-Saharan Africa remains the poorest region globally. One of the factors contributing to the limited success of foreign aid is when it comes with conditions. Unfortunately, when all the conditions are considered, the aid may not necessarily benefit the recipient's population. Foreign aid undoubtedly plays a crucial role in addressing immediate humanitarian needs and supporting development initiatives in struggling economies. However, the notion that aid alone can lift countries out of poverty, is overly simplistic and often unrealistic. [Adapted from https://businessday.ng/business-economy/article/foreign-aid]

questions.context: 2.4 Refer to the infographic on conventional energy sources in South Africa. [FIGURE: pie chart SOUTH AFRICA'S ELECTRICITY GENERATION BY SOURCE: coal 86%, other 9,1%, nuclear 4,9%. Table OVERVIEW OF SOUTH AFRICA'S NUCLEAR POWER (2023): nuclear electricity generation 8,2 TWh; reactors operable 2; reactors under construction 0; reactors proposed 2; uranium required 277 tons per year; South Africa is the world's eleventh-largest producer of uranium.] [Adapted from https://world-nuclear.org] Nuclear energy has been significant in South Africa's energy landscape for decades with the country's first and only nuclear power plant constructed in 1976 in Duynefontein, near Cape Town. Koeberg NPP, owned and operated by Eskom, has two reactors with a combined capacity of 1 869 MW. South Africa's focus on nuclear energy (as a low-carbon source of energy) is ever-increasing as the global drive towards mitigating climate change and South Africa's goal of achieving net-zero emissions becomes more pressing. However, despite the potential of nuclear production to help with the country's energy supply and meet climate goals, nuclear energy provides only 4,9% of the electricity supplied to the grid today. In South Africa, there is a historical dependency on coal due to its abundance and the economic importance of the mining industry. [Adapted from www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/latest-plans-increase-nuclear-energy-south-africa]

questions.context: 2.5 Refer to the graph and extract on energy management in South Africa. [FIGURE: bar graph TOP CO2 EMITTING COUNTRIES FROM FOSSIL FUELS (% of global emissions): China 31,5; USA 13,8; India 7,8; Russia 7,2; Japan 3,4; Germany 2,3; Indonesia 2,5; Iran 2,4; Korea 2,2; Canada 2,0; Saudi Arabia 1,9; South Africa 1,7.] THE COST OF NON-CONVENTIONAL ENERGY IN SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa is at a critical moment in its energy transition (shift): trying to decarbonise its economy and make sure that everyone has access to reliable and affordable energy. South Africa is a major carbon emitter and there is an urgent need for the country to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions. While the country has already made progress in integrating renewable energy into its power grid, its path to a sustainable energy future is complicated by financial problems and limited energy storage technology. Renewable energy sources, such as wind and solar are intermittent (erratic) and their output fluctuates. As a result, it is important to set up grid-scale storage which is very expensive. The International Partners Group has agreed to give South Africa $8,5 billion. The money aims to accelerate (quicken) the decarbonisation of South Africa's economy to help it achieve the goal of reaching net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. However, only 2,7% of the offers are grants, with the other 97% in the form of loans. [Adapted from www.mg.co.za/-the-just-energy-transition-in-south-africa/]

questions.context: SECTION B. QUESTION 3: GEOGRAPHICAL SKILLS AND TECHNIQUES. GENERAL INFORMATION ON MBOMBELA: [FIGURE: outline map of South Africa's provinces with Mbombela marked in Mpumalanga; north arrow.] Coordinates: 25° 27' 57" S; 30° 59' 07" E. Mbombela, formerly Nelspruit, is a city in northeastern South Africa. It is the capital of the Mpumalanga province. Located on the Crocodile River, the city lies about 330 km east of Johannesburg. Fertile soils and the subtropical climate provide perfect conditions for the growing of citrus and tropical fruits, mainly mango, banana, avocado, papaya and macadamia nuts. The city is a key agricultural processing hub for northeastern South Africa.
